An appropriate act omitted is an error (Arius 11a), so he acts badly (R1).

The failing is in restraining appetite and irritation, so temperance is the main virtue; endurance of hardship, which is courage, also fits (R8; Musonius in the source).

other: You see a manager in IT, who counts spending quality time with her friends and making a success of her career among the most valuable things in her life, using her abilities to be friendly, well-organised and empathic to be a good friend and an excellent manager.
self: You, a manager in IT who counts spending quality time with your friends and making a success of your career among the most valuable things in your life, use your abilities to be friendly, well-organised and empathic to be a good friend and an excellent manager.
contested_note: Epictetus's framing does not settle the verdict. 'Valuable' may mean preferred indifferents (DL 7.105), which one may rightly act for (Discourses 2.10); then the verdict is virtue. If she treats career success and time with friends as goods she must have, Handbook 19 and Discourses 2.13 make it a false judgement about externals, which would be vice. The source presents her as a pre-Stoic starting point, to be reframed by the Stoic idea of happiness. | From the vignette alone the labeller reads it as vice: Career success and time with friends are not up to us (Handbook 1: property, reputation, office). Ranking them 'among the most valuable things' places her good in externals rather than in her moral purpose (Discourses 1.29; Handbook 19), which is the error behind the citharoede's anxiety (Discourses 2.13). Her friendly, organised, empathic conduct fits her roles (R6), but an act is well done only if it comes from correct judgement (R1, Discourses 4.8), so the judgement shown makes this a failure of wisdom.

stoic_judgement: really wanting a new one now that their best friend has got a new phone (while their own phone "still works fine")
stoic_reason: The student's desire is set on property, which is not up to us (Handbook 1). The vignette ties the desire to the friend's new phone rather than to any need. Epictetus reads such a desire as the judgement that this external is a good worth envying (Handbook 19; Discourses 2.13): an assented passion, and so acting badly even with no outward deed (R1, R2). Restraint of appetite and vanity falls under temperance (R8), and failing to see what is up to us is a failure of wisdom.
